query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled in situ thermal pre-oxidation treatment that forms a robust, nano‐structured mixed HfO2/TaO2 oxide layer on the surface of cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will enhance its oxygen resistance during high‐temperature service without degrading its intrinsic mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and 163–530 MPa yield strength at 1000 °C with poor oxygen resistance.
generation.intervention: A controlled, short-duration thermal oxidation (pre-oxidation) treatment in an oxygen-containing atmosphere at approximately 1000 °C (e.g., for about 30 minutes) prior to high-temperature service.
generation.conditions: Treatment at ~1000 °C in a controlled oxygen-containing atmosphere (e.g., air) for ~30 minutes; subsequent high-temperature mechanical loading at 1000 °C under strain rates of 10^−4–10^−2 s^−1; exposure times and loading conditions matching typical service environments.
generation.structural_mediator: A dense, adherent, nano-structured passivating scale composed primarily of HfO2 and TaO2 that forms on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: The pre-formed mixed oxide scale acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion, suppressing further oxidation during high-temperature exposure. This protective layer minimizes oxygen embrittlement while preserving the cast alloy’s optimized microstructure and mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Marked improvement in oxygen resistance at high temperatures (i.e., reduced oxidation rate and slower scale degradation) with retention of baseline room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength, as compared to untreated samples.
generation.baseline: Untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy, which suffers rapid oxygen attack under high-temperature conditions, leading to embrittlement and compromised performance.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective under high-temperature static or moderately dynamic conditions (≈1000 °C, strain rates of 10^−4–10^−2 s^−1) with relatively short exposure times following pre-oxidation; its performance under prolonged cyclic thermal loading or in drastically different atmospheres remains to be established.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal treatment duration, exact temperature, and uniformity of the oxide scale formation require further experimental optimization. There is also uncertainty regarding the long-term adherence and self-healing behavior of the oxide scale under cyclic or variable loading conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HfNbTaTiZr alloy samples: one set remains in the untreated cast state and the other undergoes the controlled pre-oxidation treatment at 1000 °C in air for 30 minutes. Expose both sets to high-temperature tensile testing at 1000 °C under strain rates of 10^−4–10^−2 s^−1 for periods simulating service conditions. Conduct surface characterization (e.g., SEM, XPS) to evaluate the formation, composition, and integrity of the oxide layers, and compare oxidation-induced weight gain between the groups.
measurements: Oxide layer thickness and composition (via SEM/EDS, XPS)
Weight gain or oxidation kinetics (thermogravimetric analysis)
Tensile properties at 1000 °C (yield strength and ductility)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the pre-oxidized samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in oxidation (e.g., similar weight gain or oxide degradation) or if there is a measurable deterioration in mechanical properties (reduced ductility or yield strength) at high temperatures compared to the untreated samples.

cited_evidence.text: The NbTaHfTiZr HEA has received a lot of interests among all RHEAs, since it has a totally disordered BCC solid-solution structure with a melting point of about 1800 °C [,]. At normal temperature and cryogenic temperatures, the NbTaHfTiZr RHEA combines excellent strength and ductility []. The NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 RHEA based on this alloy not only maintains excellent room-temperature plasticity but also further improves its strength and has a good cold workability []. In order to explore the potential of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 RHEA for high-temperature applications, it is very necessary to study its mechanical properties at high temperatures. Here, we explore the mechanical properties of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy from RT to 1227 K and analyze its microscopic deformation mechanism. At the same time, we construct the constitutive equation of this alloy through a stress–strain curve in a deformation temperature range of 873–1173 K and a 0.001–0.1 s−1 strain-rate range and quantify the relationship between the strength and temperature.

In the previous results, we found that the crystal structure and microstructure of the alloy did not change significantly after rolling and heat treatment. After discussing the law of strength change with temperature and analyzing the results of the transmission electron microscopy, it is concluded that the deformation of the alloy at high temperature is mainly controlled by dislocation, and the morphology and density of the dislocation control the mechanical properties of the alloy. We have not discussed the plasticity change before, so the next focus is to analyze the change in alloy plasticity at high temperature and the reasons for that change. In high-temperature tensile tests, the strength of the alloy is more important, but the plasticity changes are equally important. In this study, it was obtained that the fracture plasticity of the alloy diminishes as the temperature rises (except at 673 K) (See Figure 4b). This trend is at odds with the experience with alloys in general, and this phenomenon may be the result of the following factors: First, the effect of high-temperature oxidation []. Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. decision.trend: Studies on the HfNbTaTiZr system and related refractory high‐entropy alloys have mainly focused on optimizing mechanical properties by fine-tuning the composition (for example, using subtraction methods to reveal elemental roles) and by processing routes (cold/hot rolling, controlled annealing) to tailor microstructure. These efforts have successfully balanced yield strength at high temperatures and room-temperature ductility. However, none have directly solved the problem of oxygen attack during high-temperature service, although some work has shown that careful control of the microstructure (and even deliberate introduction of oxygen in other HEA designs for damping benefits) can have secondary effects. The trend is clear: after composition and processing have been leveraged to secure the desirable mechanical performance, the next logical challenge is to introduce an intervention that directly stabilizes the surface behavior against oxidation while not undermining the tuned intrinsic properties.
decision.unsolved: The critical unsolved issue is that the as-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy’s poor oxygen resistance in oxygen‐containing atmospheres at high temperatures remains an obstacle. Previous interventions using additional alloying or external coatings have tended to compromise mechanical performance. There is still a lack of a single, integrated intervention that can form a robust, adherent, and protective oxide layer without sacrificing the ductility and yield strength required during high-temperature service.
decision.lever: a controlled, in situ thermal oxidation (pre‐oxidation) treatment designed to form a dense, adherent passivating oxide layer (e.g., a nano‐structured HfO2/TaO2 mixed scale) on the alloy surface
decision.why: Building on the trend where internal microstructure and composition have been optimized for mechanical properties, a surface treatment that induces a self‐passivating oxide layer is the logical next step. Such a treatment, performed at a temperature near 1000 °C in a controlled oxygen atmosphere for a defined short duration, can stabilize the surface against further oxygen uptake without altering the bulk structure. This approach leverages the inherent high-temperature stability of oxides from constituent elements and avoids the drawbacks of external coatings or full alloying modifications.

families.principle: Directly tailor the surface or interface (via coatings, pre-formed oxide layers, or interface modifications) to block oxygen diffusion, protecting the bulk without altering its intrinsic mechanical properties.
cues_for: need to avoid compromising the underlying mechanical performance
single intervention that can be applied on the as-cast alloy
cues_against: prior attempts with surface coatings have often degraded mechanical performance if the coating is too thick or poorly adherent
families.best_lever: Develop and apply an ultrathin, conformal coating—such as an atomic layer deposition (ALD) grown alumina—that forms a well-adhered, high-temperature-stable, protective surface barrier with minimal impact on the alloy’s bulk ductility and yield strength.

families.principle: Apply a post-cast heat or thermomechanical treatment to deliberately form a thin, adherent, protective oxide scale on the surface without altering the alloy’s bulk microstructure responsible for its mechanical performance.
cues_against: risk that aggressive heat treatments could alter the bulk ductility or yield strength if not carefully controlled
families.best_lever: A controlled pre-oxidation heat treatment in a mildly oxidizing atmosphere at a temperature slightly below the service temperature to form an ultra-thin, coherent protective oxide scale.

families.principle: Change the casting or synthesis procedure to modify phase distribution or elemental segregation, which in turn might favor the in situ development of oxidation‐resistant regions.
cues_against: prior approaches already include coatings or compositional adjustments that affect overall performance
families.best_lever: Optimize the casting conditions (cooling rate, mold design) to induce beneficial surface segregation of one or more elements that can form a passivating oxide layer while preserving mechanical robustness.

families.principle: Engineer the internal microstructural features (e.g., grain boundaries, phase distributions) to slow oxygen diffusion or segregation while keeping mechanical properties intact.
cues_for: cast state implies a certain microstructure that might be tuned
cues_against: no direct mention of microstructural deficiencies causing the oxygen resistance problem
difficulty in isolating surface protection from bulk modifications
families.best_lever: Refine or gradient-engineer the near-surface grain structure to act as a barrier to oxygen ingress, ensuring the bulk retains high ductility and high-temperature strength.

families.principle: Modify the alloy’s intrinsic chemical makeup to encourage the formation of a protective oxide phase (e.g., a stable alumina, chromia, or other refractory oxide) during high‐temperature exposure.
cues_against: without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance
previous approaches have considered additional alloying elements but led to degraded mechanical performance
families.best_lever: Introduce a minor, carefully optimized addition (e.g., a trace of Al) that preferentially forms a stable, protective oxide without disrupting the near‐equiatomic balance and high-temperature ductility.
